text: I am a rather elderly man, a lawyer who has spent thirty years in a snug business among rich mens bonds, mortgages, and title deeds, and of all the strange scriveners I have known, Bartleby was the strangest. <break time="0.8s" /> Of his life before he came to me nothing can be known, for, except what my own astonished eyes saw of him, there exist no materials for a full biography of the man. <break time="0.8s" /> My office stood up one flight of stairs on Wall Street, and its windows commanded, at one end, a white wall inside a light shaft and, at the other, a lofty brick wall black with age. <break time="0.8s" /> Turkey, an Englishman of about sixty, was a most valuable copyist before noon, but after his midday meal his face blazed like a coal fire, and he blotted his papers with reckless haste. <break time="0.8s" /> Nippers, a young man of five and twenty, suffered from ambition and indigestion in the mornings, when he ground his teeth over his desk, yet in the afternoons he was comparatively mild. <break time="0.8s" /> Since their fits came on in turn, like guards relieving one another, I never had to deal with both eccentricities at once, and a twelve year old boy, nicknamed Ginger Nut, ran our errands for cakes and apples. <break time="0.8s" /> When business increased, I advertised for another copyist, and one summer morning there stood upon my office threshold a motionless young man, pallidly neat, pitiably respectable, incurably forlorn. <break time="0.8s" /> Thinking that his sedate manner might have a good effect upon the flighty Turkey and the fiery Nippers, I placed his desk behind a high green folding screen, close to a small window that looked upon a wall.
